items.body:
DJ, producer and award-winning NTS host Shy One smooths out the bumps on her second album, bringing in James Massiah, Steve Spacek, George Riley and others to add color to her soulful fusion of UKF, electro and broken beat.

With records for Eglo, Numbers, Beats in Space and Scratcha's DVA Music under her belt already, Mali Larrington-Nelson, better known as Shy One, has already more than proved herself. And on 'Mali', she grows into her skin, refining the sounds she's lived with since the moment she was born - she's the daughter of Trevor Nelson, after all - and forming a narrative that's truly her own. It's a slower, more thoughtful album than its predecessor, beginning with a dusty, beatless opening track that might well feature Larrington-Nelson's mom. And on 'I Can Tell', an early single, George Riley's breathy vocals provide Larrington-Nelson with the foil she needs for her intricate, swaying beats. It's gear that splits the difference between Crazy Cousinz and Katy B, hitting the all the right pop notes without losing its underground edge.

Instrumentals like 'Loosen Up' and 'Nort Wess', the album's first single, might be even better, with the latter effectively bridging the gap between grime and Drexciyan electro, slowing down the usual tempo and chopping synth stabs and derailed, underwater effects into the bass squelches and syncopated kicks. Steve Spacek's appearance on 'Driving On Sand' is appreciated, mind you, when he brings gospel-like levity to Larrington-Nelson's electric piano stabs and acidic squelches. Really, the album's a love letter to properly soulful bass music in all its forms, and there's no better person to shepherd us to the next epoch.

items.body:
French musical outlaw Pascal Comelade presents a selection of eccentric covers recorded over the last four decades, including madcap versions of classics from Nirvana, The Kinks, Captain Beefheart, MC5, The Ramones and Bob Dylan.

Since the '70s, Comelade has been questioning the logic of so-called experimental music, using cheap instruments like singing saws, recorders and toy pianos to make covers of modern standards - rock songs, easy listening earworms - that flip expectations. If you've never come across his solo productions or his work with his legendary Bel Canto Orquestra, then 'Métaphysique Du Hit-Parade' is the ideal introduction - a selection of Comelade's finest covers with a couple of brand new ones (junkshop versions of Dylan's 'Girl from the North Country' and Nirvana's 'Come As You Are') thrown in for good measure. 

Now none of this should work on any metric, but there's an earnestness to Comelade's music that makes it hit surprisingly hard. Just check the hideously detuned bontempi version of 'Sunny Afternoon' and try not to crack a smile, or his ramshackle take on 'Purple Haze'. It ain't pretty, but it works.

items.body:
Rachel Grimes and Jefre Cantu-Ledesma collaborator Christopher Tignor deploys an anti-AI statement with 'Bleeding Past the Edge', performing the album in real time to display his humanity.

It's too easy, we suppose, to create music that's an assemblage of layered parts, loops and samples - if we can do it relatively frictionlessly, then surely a computer can embark on the same painless journey, too. That's what drove Tignor to create his latest record, working in his small studio with custom software, his violin, some tuning forks and pedals. He wanted to create an "immersive, orchestral sound" live, with just a single performer, without relying on loops and backing tracks, so developed the system that's displayed here. Honestly, we probably wouldn't know unless you told us, but there's at least a refreshing looseness to the rhythms of Tignor's 'Shadow Purposes' tracks, once the fusty opener 'Weight of Words' is out of the way.

items.body:
New LP from Pye Corner Audio via Sonic Cathedral.

"Pye Corner Audio releases a new album, More Songs About The Sun, on June 19. It’s his second studio album for Sonic Cathedral and a sequel of sorts to 2022’s acclaimed Let’s Emerge!. The title is a light-hearted acknowledgment that the album picks up exactly where the last one ended with ‘Warmth Of The Sun’, with opener ‘Euphoria’ mixing blissed-out Balearica with guitars by labelmate (and Ride / Oasis member) Andy Bell. “I definitely wanted it to feel like a direct continuation from the previous one,” explains Pye Corner Audio, aka Martin Jenkins. “I wanted the whole record to be awash with distortion and saturation, but not in a blown-out guitar amp kind of way.” He’s right: everything here feels a lot bigger, bolder and acid bright. “The musical influences are all the usual suspects – Stereolab, Spacemen 3, Harmonia, Cluster, Suicide,” he reveals. “But I think that this album wears them in a much more direct way.”

Several songs feature vocals, and not all by Martin himself – ‘The Breath Of Now’ has a stunning, spoken word monologue by Scottish crime writer Ian Rankin. The resulting dystopian nightmare is the first time that clouds of darkness obscure the sunshine, but, as Martin says, “you need the shade to appreciate the sun”. “If there’s a theme that runs throughout then it’s optimism, even in these darkened days. The sun will continue to rise… even if there’s no one around to see it.”"

items.body:
A sequel to 2024's rock history redux 'This is BASIC', the spartan 'BASIC' boasts a new lineup, featuring Tortoise's Doug McCombs, and introduces Tuareg and Highlife rhythms while retaining the electroacoustic bent of their debut.

'This is BASIC' was a great idea handled very well; the project was initiated by Chris Forsyth and Nick Millevoi as a reaction to Robert Quine and Fred Maher's 'Basic', a hypnotic mid-'80s cult classic that welded nascent drum machine loops to post-punk guitar phrases. The two players wondered if there was a way that thread might be followed a few decades later and invited Mikel Patric Avery to help out with the electronics. Since then, Millevoi has dropped out but he's been replaced by McCombs, who initially crewed up to help the band tour their debut and ended up sticking around for recording afterwards.

As you might expect, 'BASIC' skews a little more post-rock than its predecessor, with McCombs' signature playing front and center, at least at first, but the band do their best to keep folding in fresh influences, charting a course where guitar music wasn't constantly being deconstructed and reinvented to harmonize with cultural waves. Forsythe's usage of Tuareg riffs is particularly effective (check 'Loose Cannon') and puts a completely different spin on McCombs' basslines and 'Index of Memories' is fascinating, a whirring mass of xenharmonic synth flutes, skipping beats and druggy guitar lines that sounds like it's about to be pounced on by Pete Swanson and Jed Bindeman's Freedom To Spend imprint.

items.body:
Oren Ambarchi's kraut-techno-free jazz magnum opus is back for its 10th anniversary -  an ambitious ensemble piece featuring an all-star list of players including Ricardo Villalobos, Keith Fullerton Whitman, Mark Fell, crys Cole, Will Guthrie, Arto Lindsay and Konrad Sprenger... Wooooo

You've got to admire Ambarchi's chutzpah here. 'Hubris' is an all you can eat buffet of his various musical cravings, a chance for his friends, influences and collaborators to flex a little and for Ambarchi to attempt to ride the groove like an experienced cowboy on an out-of-control bucking bronco. The first side is the biggest surprise, a dedication to Wang Chung's enduring, disco-influenced 'To Live and Die in L.A.' soundtrack that begins with ping-ponging guitar notes and Jim O'Rourke's synth blips, before elusive Berlin-based composer Konrad Sprenger (aka Joerg Hiller) drops in with some motorized guitar vamps. It's rhythmic gear that fits in with the Berlin school until Mark Fell appears in the final third with some typically fractured percussion.

On the flip, the groove loosens after a short guitar interlude. Ricardo Villalobos takes over with a suitably winding, minimal throb over live rhythms played by Joe Talia and Will Guthrie simultaneously as krautrock techno mutates into disco fusion. Keith Fullerton Whitman tries to nudge the track off the rails with his modular expositions, but the path is set - Arto Lindsay's axe is just the icing on the cake. By the end of the side, we're in full jazz-noise mode: everything's still pegged to Villalobos' central pulse, but that's the only element that's bolted down. 

Hard to believe it's 10 years already - we can't think of a better skeleton key to unlock the secrets behind Black Truffle's musical identity.

items.body:
Gathering the short-lived Boston emo outfit's influential debut 'Junk', shoegaze-y sophomore album 'This Afternoon Malady', the unfinished third album and everything in-between, 'Wait A Lifetime' will be crucial listening if you're more than a casual Jejune fan.

Jejune were never the Berklee-educated New England scene's best band, but they proved their mettle all the same, penning a pair of albums that almost inadvertently steered the course of the emo underground. Those records aren't without their faults, sure, but it's hard to get an accurate read on the US scene without them. And they've never sounded better; with a fresh lick of paint, 'Junk' and its superior, if way more misunderstood follow-up deserves to be filed alongside Karate's early records at the very least. And for the heads, 'Wait A Lifetime' sweeps up all the band's recorded material, the loose singles, split EPs and compilation tracks, even excavating the sessions from their aborted third album and commissioning an essay from critic Nina Corcoran to fill in the gaps.

items.body:
Their first project as a duo, 'Midmeste' is Aussie composer-performers and long time collaborators Judith Hamann and James Rushford's latest slow-mo meditation on musical history, psychoacoustic phenomena and minimalism, performed on cello and various pipe organs.

Hamann and Rushford have been working together for years, most visibly alongside Sam Dunscombe as Golden Fur, a chamber ensemble the friends established back in 2008. Each artist has moved decisively in the time since: Berlin-based Hamann outdid herself on last year's intimate and deeply personal 'Aunes', while Rushford brought his various experiments to a focal point on 'Turzets', balancing his tongue-in-cheek electroacoustic experiments with bold medieval deconstructions. Working as a duo, the pair isolate the similarities in their respective musical signatures; the title is a Middle English word meaning "the middlemost point" and signals the album's creation, where they searched out creative overlaps: xenharmonic tunings, organology, psychoacoustics and unintentional sounds, just for starters. And knowing each other so well is also a boon. Where so much minimal avant-garde gear can sound stuffy to the point of being exclusionary, 'Midmeste' sounds inviting even at its most uncompromising.

They use English early music composer John Dunstaple's 'O rosa bella' to anchor their experiments, returning to its core themes every time the album starts to veer too far off course. And there's a refreshing calmness to this technique; in the beginning, Hamann's piercing harmonics provide the edge, while Rushford's rounded organ chords welcome in a more familiar structure that Hamann respects with elegant cello tones. Interestingly, the duo were given the opportunity to record the world's oldest playable organ, a 15th century instrument at Basilica St Valere in Switzerland. Since they were both on residency at La Becque in Lake Geneva, it made perfect sense to document the organ's unique character and add it to their composition - contextually, it's right on point. Mid-way through the first side, we can hear its creaking, crackling wooden frame and whistling resonances, the puffing bellows and the sound of hands and feet on the instrument.

It's these impeccably captured peripheral sounds that give us a sense of place, bolstering the duo's engagement with history with a tangible historical object that still tells us its age. Tones warble, wobble and boom through the centuries-old pipes and Hamann follows the course with her patient, literate responses that add romance, mystery and humanity to what, on its own, might be dry. So we end up with forty minutes of some of the most unashamedly beautiful music either artist has put their name to yet - 'Midmeste' is a duet that whisks you through time, physical space and tonality itself. Remarkable stuff.

items.body:
MEGO mainstay Tujiko Noriko returns to the label for her sixth venture, a double-album celebration of her cat Pon that's brimming with eccentricity and positivity. It's pop music on some level, but anchored by cinematic whimsy and the unique production touches that have had us following her every move for the last quarter century. RIYL Björk, Tenniscoats, Astrid Sonne, Julia Holter, Ichiko Aoba.

Films have always had an influence on Noriko's music; in 2005, she even embarked on a film career in earnest, working on various experimental films until her proper feature 'Kuro' had matured to completion in 2017. So it's hardly surprising that her experience with film soundtracks - she handled the score for 2020's 'Surge' and 2024's 'He's Watching You' - has impacted her solo work. Her last album, the sublime 2LP elegy 'Crépuscule I & II' was an attempt by Noriko to collide her two creative worlds, meditating on nocturnal themes that seemed to hum with widescreen energy. And this latest record picks up where it left off, looking back over her relationship with her cat Pon who recently died in an accident. 'Pon' is a poppier record than its predecessor and doesn't dwell on sadness; its cinematic cues are hopeful, light and affecting, sculpted expertly by Noriko to give weight to her inner voice, the naive, intimate utterances that have characterized her music since the very beginning.

At first, it's not clear where we're headed. 'Only on Love', the album's skittering opening track, galvanizes Noriko's classic sound, letting her half-whispered vocals soar across pitchy drones and slow, metallic glitches. Noriko introduces us to the pop side of her personality first, with cool-headed, languid wordless hooks (check the gorgeous 'Bosom') and tight cybernetic rhythms that split the difference between Matmos and Pan Sonic. But by the time we reach 'Kikoeru Pon' ("hearing Pon"), the tone has begun to shift; using environmental recordings and neoclassical flourishes inspired by Nicholes Britell's enduring 'If Beale Street Could Talk' cue 'Agape', Noriko brings hope into the mix, ushering us into her IRL space, where we can hear rain on the window and Pon purring. And it's this alchemical blend that makes 'Pon' so touching - using the emotional language she's learned from cinema, Noriko is able to spirit us away into Pon's world and her own, a fantasy space that's both tiny and theatrically immense.

On 'Knife of Yonder', that space is dreamlike and billowing, stretched out over 11 minutes of analog moans and evocative bursts of percussion, while on 'Beachside Cats', the album transforms into lighthearted tropical psychedelia, offering a palate cleanser before the dramatic high-point 'Bokuno Satellite', a fusion of wailing noirish theremins, sunny guitars, "easy listening" vibraphones and chipmunked vocal stutters. Like its predecessor, 'Pon' is a lengthy proposition, but Noriko keeps it moving by constantly morphing; like a film that assembles its various stylistic chunks into a devastating whole (we're looking at you, 'Resurrection'), the album benefits from repeat listens, where its set-pieces can be deconstructed with the knowledge of each devastating buildup and release. As Ebert and Siskel might have said: two thumbs up.

items.body:
A new set of unreleased sessions from Sun Ra's prolific early 1970s period bundled with two '80s live jams, 'East Two +7' is one for fans of Ra's off-world electronic material - ie. his most vital shit.

Honestly, you'd win us over with the fifteen minute 'East Two' alone. The 15-minute track was recorded in Chicago's Streeterville Studios in 1972 and emerged during a fertile period for Ra, towards the end of his time on New York City's avant-garde circuit. That year he dubbed 'Space is the Place', 'Universe in Blue' and the Moog-augmented sidestep 'Discipline 27-II', and that was only the beginning. Ra and his collaborators spent two days in Streeterville and went deep; Ra played synth, Pat Patrick was on bass, Kwame Hadi played trumpet and John Gilmore handled the tenor horn. And Ra's contribution is subtle at first; he hangs back, playing dissonant, sci-fi tinged tones behind his bandmates' wilder, bendier solos before lurching forward, jamming out nasty organ runs and unhinged oscillations before the track grinds to a halt.

Elsewhere, there's the 1973 track 'In Tomorrow's Realm', where Ra plays against the Arkestra's Ronnie Boykins on bass and an unravelled version of 'Yesterdays' that was recently discovered on an unlabelled reel-to-reel tape, featuring Ra on the Yamaha YC-30 combo organ. Even the two live recordings, a version of the 'Omniverse' favorite 'The Place of Five Points' captured in Columbus, Ohio in 1985 and a 'Fate in a Pleasant Mood' pit dub from the Arkestra's 1984 tour through Egypt and Europe, are worth checking into.

items.body:
Andrew Field-Pickering (aka Max D) and Matt Papich (aka Co La) consider the process of filmmaking on their fifth album, adding foley sounds, concrète, and snatched conversations to their loose-limbed melange of Jazz, post rock and dub soundscapes, featuring additional players more eaze, Motion Graphics, Dustin Wong, Jeremy Hyman and more to complete the picture. Anyone on the line from Tortoise to Conjoint - we urge you to check in.

Lifted’s last album 'Trellis', arrived on Peak Oil following a run of deployments for PAN and Max D's own Future Times imprint and took stock of their run until that point, a surreal collage of studio recordings with input from a few trusted collaborators - all of whom also appear on 'Movie'. But this new set feels more like a line in the sand, a statement record that focuses the core duo's skills around a loose concept: cinema. Woven into a very TNT-esque post rock landscape, the duo weave overlapping dialog, room recordings and found sounds, referencing the kind of multi-track recording style that helped Robert Altman bring 'Nashville' to life, as well as Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s “slow cinema" style, focusing on seemingly insignificant sound details in the mix.

On ‘The Ice Chewers' Field-Pickering and Papich put more eaze to good use, backing up her bass guitar, pedal steel and acoustic guitar parts with an arsenal of FX and broken drums. Using tape stop effects to pitch the material as if putting their thumb on the master, the duo sound as if they're tinkering with the reel, burning it out just like Ingmar Bergman did in 'Persona' to remind you it was all celluloid. Musically, it's again a throwback to Tortoise's enduring 'TNT', letting it dissolve completely before hitting us with the noir-ish 'Paranoids'. Here, foley sounds overlap with indistinct dialog and environmental echoes that the duo loop and echo, painting an indistinct picture of a film that might be as eerie as 'The Conversation' or as eroticised as 'Klute'. 

On 'Repossessed' they shift into chillier territory and nattily avoid the churned Carpenterisms that have been rinsed to an almost laughable extent for the last few decades. Their VHS gore-inspired 'Melts Very Nasty' also avoids the obvious route, hinting at the general aura by using Mezey and Motion Graphics' submerged synths and Moore's bagpipes for added tension. They even hold back a genuine belter for the end credits: the soft rock-inspired 'Midnight Snack' - a 5 minute coda that could have been an after-hours Prince jam back in the day. Basically, even if you think you've got a lid on Lifted, 'Movie' really takes things to another level.

items.body:
A true ‘80s evergreen, Wally Badarou’s debut LP is perhaps best known for lending a huge hook to Massive Attack, but the rest is gold, too! Ten dreamy, sexy, synth instrumentals that sound timelessly fresh as ever, over 40 years later. Big RIYL Ryuichi Sakamoto, The Wild Bunch, Grace Jones, Bill Laswell/Material.

Faithfully replicating the Island Records pressing of ’84, ‘Echoes’ returns to vinyl circulation after a decade or so with the sound of an eternal summer. Whether you know it for the slinky ‘Mambo’, which was lifted almost wholesale for Massive Attack’s ‘Daydreaming’, or via Balearic or downbeat circles, the music’s appeal surely spans generations. 

Fair to say it’s future-proofed by a type of sophisticated, breezy but dead tight rhythm programming comparable with YMO’s Sakamoto or Hosono of that era, all chiffon-layered, heat hazy synth lustre, vivid melodies and supremely buttered grooves, balanced with a blend of romantic frisson and experimental studio urges.

Subtropical winds fill the sails of ‘Keys’, and canny measures of Linn-cracked Afrobeat groove and concrète collage commingle on ‘Hi-Life’, demonstrating subtle studio flourishes that are woven into the vocoder of ‘Voices’, while ‘Endless Race’ feels like Yello doing a Caribbean TV theme, and ‘Rain’ signs off with a cinematic chef’s kiss of piano & pads hinting at his Gallic background and intention to write the “soundtrack to an imaginary movie.”

items.body:
Adrian Rew's properly hypnotic cult classic 'Slot Machine Music' has finally been reissued and it sounds even more terrifying and prescient than it did back in 2013 at the height of the basement noise era. One of the best environmental recording records bar none - don't sleep.

Back in 2009, PAN released its fourth album, 'Kenrimono', a set of recordings made by Greek sound artist Ilios at Japanese pachinko halls. The sheer density of it was as shocking and as intense as anything the noise genre had to offer, packed out with whirring, crunching and chiming resonances that took you to the smokey epicenter of the Japanese gambling world. And when 'Slot Machine Music' arrived a few short years later we assumed the sound would be similar; we were wrong. Initially dropped via Rew's own Ergot Records on CDr before the great Aaron Dilloway stepped in to handle the vinyl edition on his own Hanson imprint, the album seemingly grew from the Midwestern noise petri dish - but it wasn't an exercise in aesthetic posturing, using the racket of the modern American casino to mimic the intensity of a Wolf Eyes set. Instead, Rew was drawn to the experience itself, that's been meticulously designed by malign forces to guide behavior: those trapped inside the casino's four walls are seduced into spending more, losing more and returning to do it all over again.

Rew didn't know much about the environment when he visited Cleveland's Horseshoe Casino for the first time in 2013 armed with an Olympus LS-11 recorder and a camera. And over four months, he developed a peculiar relationship with the culture, surreptitiously taping the soundscapes at various Midwestern locations - in Michigan, Indiana, Ohio and Illinois - while attempting not to lose too much cash in the process. And it's a warts-n-all set, with dialog snippets and outdoor ambiance giving us more than simply the dense mass of chimes and stings and themes that you'd hear on the casino floor itself. What Rew is able to do is create a snapshot of a time and place, capturing the sheer desolation of the casino experience and using it to drive a narrative that Robert Altman would be proud of. The first thing you notice is that each machine's sounds are in tune with the next; "game designers," explains Rew, "tune their machines to the key of C in order to optimize harmonic cohesion." So although Rew's recordings are full-bodied, they're never too chaotic or discordant. 

Indeed, if you check in for the entire record - 2013's iconic 'Slot Machine Music' and its 2014 sequel 'Slot Machine Music Vol. 2' - you'll be lulled into the same false sense of security that entrances casino regulars. It's almost like ambient music, packed out with tiny sonic details that some well-paid sound engineer-cum-neurologist worked for years to figure out. Guided meditation music? New age crypto-psychedelia? It's all here, packaged in neon-lit one-armed-bandits aimed to target the dopamine centers of aging boomers with money to burn. And the best thing about the recordings is that Rew keeps some of the chatter intact, so we can hear him tangling with casino security, or haggling with his slot machine neighbors over change. We can hear the cheers and claps as paltry sums are won while vast fortunes are lost. The best moment for us comes when Rew wanders outside Grand Victoria Casino in Elgin, Illinois at the dead of night, the crickets singing as the machines echo from behind grand double doors. A freight train rushes past and blots out any other sound, distorting the recording.

It's a good reminder that although you might be able to hide from reality inside the casino, the Midwest will inevitably confront you with its rusted truth.

items.body:
On his dank solo debut LP, proper, Bristol dubstep OG Kahn trusts in the old ways for a raft of halfstep suffused with heavy energies from Giallo OSTs, goth rock, Memphis rap, and trip hop

One of those rare things, a strong dubstep long player, ‘Past Life’ weighs in a definitive self-portrait of Kahn that speaks as much to his 16 years of skin in the game, as much as his broader tastes for mood-driven musick often associated with Bristol’s wellspring of styles & patterns. The eight tracks consolidate formative tastes with contemporary confidence in his sound design tekkerz, balancing inch-tight programming with a crucial feel for negative space and macabre gloom that makes it a wholly enveloping album experience top to bottom. 

After duo and trio LPs since 2015 with Neek, Commodo & Gantz, this one really gets under the skin of Kahn’s sound to achieve his intent, to make an album that, in his own words, “felt aligned with that sound I was exploring back in the early days”, and which falls back “into that older version of my musical identity. My past life, if you like.” As such it cleaves much closer to fundamentals of ’06 era dubstep than the “brostep” era he first emerged into, holding a light to what originally made the sound so distinctive, and relatable to other stylishly darkside musics. 

In procession from the dread cyber noir of ‘Curfew’, thru the timber shiver triplet saccades of ‘Drawing Breath’, via explicit nods to his cues in the carmine-stained atmosphere of ‘Giallo’, the sewer-dancing wraith ‘Totentanz’, and a mighty title tune nodding to earliest DMZ and Skull Disco, it’s damn sturdy session by one of the sound’s key 2nd wave standard bearers.

items.body:
Soul Jazz Records celebrate 25 years of working in partnership with Studio One with these brand-new editions of seven of their best-selling classic Studio One singles, all released for the first time ever on special edition one-off pressing groovy coloured vinyl 7”s

Heart-melting, late ‘60s rocksteady-soul by an early iteration of roots reggae legends, The Abyssinians - the Manning siblings aka Studio One greats, Carlton & The Shoes. Repressed due to demand, Soul Jazz pair the A-side of their debut, the gorgeous staple ‘Love Me Forever’, with its swoon-worthy vocal harmonies and dusted shuffle, to the more haunting, dubbed-out B-side ‘Never Let Go’, rendering the harmonies wider and more spectral on a slow, barrelling bassline. Pure gold: cop two - one for you and one for a lover.

items.body:
Rattly, stripped-to-the-bone IDM gear that harks back to simpler times, BOT1500's second proper album is simple and elegant, more concerned with the emotional weight of its melodies than the complexity of its beats.

You might remember Shinichi Koboyashi's last BOT1500 album 'Surreal', that appeared back in 2022 on AD93's Lith Dolina sublabel. And since then he's been relentlessly prolific on his Bandcamp, issuing regular single track updates that chart his creative process. But 'The Black Sea' is his first longer set in a while, assembling a handful of tracks that highlight his recent interest in minimalism, emotion and dub production techniques. The familiar monosynth groans and dry, jazzy breaks on 'Abstract Springs' might resemble Squarepusher for a moment, but it's much chillier, sparser gear, with space around each element that softens the impact of the hyperactive edits. And on 'Shadows', that same mood pervades the track even when the beats have been silenced; Koboyashi gives just as much importance to his chiming analog synths, coaxing out fragile melodies that sound as if they've been plucked out of time.

And there's a precision to his programming that's immediately impressive. On 'XB 1', his soft focus glitches and woody hits graze the post-dubstep landscape but subtly reframe it, setting the meticulous rhythms against echoing single note sine hits and melancholy pads. And the track's sequel 'XB 2' is an even harder punch to the gut, with exquisite melodies and knife-edge drums that shuttle us right back to 1996 for a moment, an underground dominated by Clear Records, Spymania and Rephlex.

items.body:
Heat Crimes’ exceptional mixtape series lands its third instalment, this time featuring a DJ from Brasilia of Lebanese heritage - DJ Patwa -  exploring Arabic influence on Brazilian baile, parading 70 minutes of upfront favela funk liberally spiced with Arabic vocal idents and licks. Crucial, contemporary aural anthropology from one of the world’s greatest underground labels, no less! Massive RIYL DJ K, Anderson Do Paraiso, xavisphone, Ramon Sucesso.

An utterly fascinating study in modern Brazilian baile culture and its historic providence, DJ Patwa’s ‘Harara Baile’ homes in on the way Arab culture contributes to the hugely distinct flavour of Brazilian ghetto dance music. On the most immediate level it serves combustible party fuel, but more intentionally speaks to a near millennia of Moorish influence on the Iberian peninsula, and the mass immigration of Syrians & Lebanese in the early C.20th, as well as the difficult histories of enslaved Muslim Africans absorbed into Brazilian culture. 

In sides centred on the sounds of ‘Harara’ (Arabic for “Heat”) from Rio, and São Paolo’s ‘Jara’im’ (“Crimes”), Arabic samples are severed from religious connotation and used for the aesthetic properties that also appeal to any non-arabic user. Yet it also represents ironic, counter-cultural snooks at US hegemony, as in the tunes of Baile da Arábia - a wing of criminal faction Comando Vermelho (or CV, as surveyed on Sublime Frequencies’ SF038 in 2007), who are titled for anti-imperialist sentiments shared with the Arab world  - and the use of handles such as MC Bin Laden (now MC Binn) or DJ Sorriso Talibã, or in the emergence of the Magrão beat sound, characterised in DJ Blakes’ ‘Magrão Arábico’, for example. 

‘Harara Baile’ is to be taken as raw, living, expressive cultural artefact that does not belong in a museum, but firmly on the ‘floor, at street raves, and booming from car boots. Lyrics about everyday favela life - sex, death, drugs, crime - can be heard to mirror gangster rap (if you understand Portuguese), but with their own accent and set to very particular rhythms on a ‘Harara’ half focussed on 150-180 BPM carioca heat from Rio, thru the more rudely psychoactive and distorted, staccato sound of modern-day São Paolo surveyed on its ‘Jara’im’ side. 

It’s all among the fiercest testaments to the game-changing modernism of Brazilian music in the 2020s, and thus acutely advised to lovers of new music who appreciate that little evolves in a vacuum or under conservative cultures - just look at so much staid Western dance music dominated by rote bores; it just doesn’t compare to the thrills of this stuff.

items.body:
30 year reissue of Dylan Carlson and co.’s ’96 drone doom masterwork, still packing thee heaviest riffs this side of Sunn O))) and Black Sabbath - from whom they cadged the name, Earth.

If there was a doom drone rock hall of fame, ‘Pentastar: In The Style Of Demons’ would be mantled in there along with Earth’s preceding Subpop sides, ‘Earth 2 (Special Low Frequency Version)’ and ‘Phase 3: Thrones and Dominions.’ The 1996 album would mark the end of an inspirational run that effectively reduced heavy metal to its bass elements whilst managing to not slosh out the baby with the bathwater; maintaining umbilical links to the blues and heavy rock via its alchemic mutation at the hands of Brummie yobs, and subsequent afterlife in their native north west corner of America.

Between the anticipatory guillotine riffs of their crushing ‘Introduction’ and its reprise in ‘Coda Maestro In F (Flat) Minor’ (which was also later remixed, surprisingly subtly, by Autechre), they churn up pure, slow-motion heck on the swag of ‘High Command’ and single “hit” of ‘Tallahassee’, bleaching out into darkly sublime drone tension with ‘Crooked Axis For String Quartet,’ before steering the sound to medieval folk on ‘Charloteer (Temple Song),’ and stark piano chamber musick of ’Sonar and Depth Charge.’ 

One for the journey.

items.body:
Field Records’ treasured Monolake reissue program yields a first vinyl cut of the influential project’s 2nd album - the last as a duo of Robert Henke & Gerhard Behles, before the latter turned attention wholly to developing Ableton Live software. Genuine landmark stuff for electronica fiends

In suit with the reissued ‘Hong Kong’ (1997) comp of early EPs for Chain Reaction, and the self-released debut LP ‘Gravity’ (2001), comes ‘Interstate’; one of Monolake’s most distinctive entries in the space where dub techno met concrète sound design and hypermodern electronica. The 65 minute album sees Henke & Behles ultimately conclude a vision of a semi-organic techno architecture that transcends club, home, and can listening, thanks to their judicious balance of whirring, syncopated grooves and custom-built, elemental sound design that feels remarkably future-proofed, then and now, 

In historic terms the duo follow a line of activated electronic systems from David Tudor to Lee “Scratch” Perry, Vince Clarke to Uwe Schmidt, Basic Channel and Autechre, by breathing vivid, imaginary life and space into circuitry and code. More specifically, in Monolake’s hands, everything teems with insectoid detail and a fascinating depth perception, conjuring immersive environments one can take as much pleasure from dancing to as simply admiring its elegantly awesome architexture. 

The relatively new freedoms of Max/MSP software and the pair’s ever heightened proprioception allowed them to enact forms of impossible physics that dance into hyperspace between the air-stepping lushness of ‘abundance’ and needlepoint D&B abstractions ‘ginza’ or ‘terminal’, showcasing sheer, advanced tekkerz on ‘gecko’ and serving the ‘floor with nexx-level depths on two parts of ‘tangent’, plus the metallic electro ping-pong of ‘perpetuum’ and 10 mins of proto-virtual reality in ‘amazon.’

items.body:
Supremely heavyweight 3+ hours of Phill Niblock’s immense instrumental slabs  - essential listening for disciples of Éliane Radigue, Tony Conrad, Kevin Drumm, Sunn 0))), Eleh.

R.I.P

First presented in 2006, ‘Touch Three’ showcases 9 pieces, 3hr 33min of material recorded and processed by Niblock between 2003-2005. Aside to its ‘sax Mix’, all works were produced from the sound of one player, on one instrument, into a sole mic, whose recordings were edited of breathing spaces with a Powerbook G4 to leave only the natural decay and attack of their tones. All straightforward enough, but the results are powerfully transcendent, producing sustained microtones that uncannily resemble electronic sources yet are entirely acoustic in nature. 

In effect the works induce an acute sense of suspense on the cusp of calm and dread, favouring the sort of resonances that one recognises from the “real” world, although exaggerated. In the process his organised sounds connote the feel of horror films as much as the hypnagogia of riding heavy machinery such as a bus or more pertinently a motorbike, the latter of which, along with the music of Morton Feldman, initially inspired Niblock - a photographer and pioneering Intermedia artist by trade - to start arranging sound in the ‘70s.

It’s safe to say that Niblock’s music effortlessly aids one in achieving rarer states of mind. Given due attention (it more often demands, not requests it), it holds great potential to inspire sensations of synaesthesia and short circuit audio-visual, spatio-temporal perceptions like few others.

items.body:
MBM & Merzbow rattle out side-long collisions of breakbeats and jagged, atonal tumult playing to both artist’s signature styles, for the industrial diehards at Cold Spring...

"'Extinct' sees the duo take listeners on a transcendental journey, focusing on the dismantling of beat and structure and recycling the result through layers of beautifully crafted noise and feedback loops, giving birth to new rhythms buried deep in the dirt.

"We may not speak the same language, but in the vortex of sound, there's a raw, primal understanding that transcends words. Noise can be art, a visual representation could maybe be Jackson Pollock's No 5, a plexus of chaos redefining what music can and could be. Pushing boundaries with Masami wasn't just a musical adventure, it was a masterclass in sonic anarchy" (Jack Dangers, January 2024).

The 20 minute opener 'FLAKKA' takes constantly evolving breakbeats which are gradually broken down over time, driven through a filter of harsh noise, destroying the old to give birth to the new. Raw and unforgiving, the track is a behemoth that blends mutant forms of broken beats and hints of dub, creating rhythmic noise of the highest calibre in the process.

'Burner' takes the record to its ultimate conclusion, the initial drum beat broken down so that it is barely recognisable. Pulsating distortion and high end audio fragments bleed into each other as the track lumbers forth and destroys everything in its path before slowly unravelling, degrading and falling apart.

A harrowing yet somewhat cathartic trip through walls of harsh industrial noise and audio degradation, 'Extinct' is a masterful pairing of artists who have delivered something truly unique yet totally relevant. Don't sleep on this one! (Todd Robinson / Subunit)."

Originally released in 2009, Capri is a concept album composed of fragmented vignettes, lost minutes and scenes from an idyllic imagining.

"A collection of brief moments, suspended shimmers, and frail settings, Capri was never meant to be more than its own thin veneer; a naked and subtle wash of saturated and semi-transparent colors, rolling as gently as ocean waves against rocky beaches, of fading afternoon sunlight, of momentary experience. Peaceful yet isolated, quiet yet collapsing, they are fading moments without definite borders, directions, or conclusion.

Remastered by Stephan Mathieu from the original tapes, and expanded to include the complete recordings excluded from the 2009 CD edition, this collection is finally present in its complete form in the deluxe edition. All music by Danielle Baquet and Will Long, 2007-2008."

items.body:
Detroit’s leading astrofuturist goes all-in on with a 76 minute odyssey taking in his slinkiest variants of Afro-Latinate techno, spangled synth kaos, syncopated bleep fields, Sun Ra-esque space jazz and one of his most widescreen visions in ‘March of the Purple Orbs’, plus interplanetary steppas on ‘Terraform’ and ‘Circumstellar Debris’.

 

"To this day, Earthlings have managed to dodge some of nature's more dangerous extremities, massive volcanic eruptions, Earthquakes, solar burst that knocked out the Planet's entire electrical grid for 3 years, numerous plagues of disease, food and fresh water shortages, domestic and International Wars and many other life-changing operas, but for this event, what remains is a realization that has no remedy. The cause: Earth's physicality has changed. It is no longer favorable for living things.

It is the constant shifting of the planet's internal tectonic plates which has unfortunately produced an unexpected and impassable dilemma.

Because of the collisions, deep within the planet's core, the planet is now producing an extraordinary amount of sound that includes a specific harmonic frequency that erodes the natural senses of all life on Earth.

It is intensifying. It is intolerable and it is unlivable.

Yet, some humans prefer to stay, to "ride it out" like the Titanic captain going down with his ship. Some, in total disbelief as some have concluded it is the second coming of Jesus Christ. But for most, the decision is clear. To live another day, leaving is the only rational choice.

At an increasing rate, scientific research data shows that humans and most animals, excluding the Jellyfish will eventually lose the usage of hearing and are to greatly suffer from an array of other neurological and psychological effects. The sense of touch and taste, sleep depreciation, severe nerve damage, constant hallucinations. Everyone will lose many of their cognitive abilities within an estimated 12 months from now.

On this day and every 7 days afterwards until all registered passengers have departed, the first of a fleet of large numbers of massive size spacecraft carrying approximately 1 million humans per vessel will permanently leave Earth to begin the long and adventurous trek across outer space to a new home: Vega. This is not a precautionary tale as there is nothing to learn. Instead, a decision has been made and a Trip To Vega is the consequence.

- Jeff Mills"

items.body:
Estonia’s reliable club freqs at Porridge Bullet bypass expectations with two cuts of raw black metal heck by a pair of artists moonlighting from usual styles

As black metal is practically pop in the Baltic and Scandi regions (well, kinda), Tapetud Rott’s furnace blasts of detuned guitars, gloom-ridden vibes and scorched vox aren’t totally out of place, yet still make a strong sore thumb on a label best known for its odd funk and dub. Perhaps closest to the likes of Ratkiller on the label (Tapetud Rott translates to killed rat), the duo of Mikk Madisson & Robert Nikolajev fully commit to the BM sound on both counts, going sludgy, slow and bloodthirsty on ‘See mees’, and full bore with the blast beats and throttled axes of ‘Lähme õue’, sealed with helldog vox.

items.body:
Oren Ambarchi offers a necessary new vinyl edition of his 'Grapes From The Estate' classic on Black Truffle. Out of print on any format for years, it’s a pleasure to see and hear this new reissue in the flesh, and to be reminded of when its floating harmonic tones first deeply seduced us and our friends. True to say its lost none of its capacity to soothe and absorb listeners like few other records we can think of. A proper modern drone evergreen.

“Oren Ambarchi's third solo project for Touch [after Suspension and Insulation] sees him reaching beyond the work for electric guitar that he's become recognised for, expanding his palette and taking his investigations into another sphere entirely. Grapes from the Estate features new instrumentation (strings, tuned bells, percussion and others that can only be guessed at), but the singular and unmistakable influence that Ambarchi exerts on these new materials is what makes it such an indelible work. 

There is a reconciliation of his love of song-based music and his determination to deal in pure sound. The result is a work that truly eludes such arbitrary definitions. Grapes From The Estate is an all consuming experience that draws the listener out of an ordinary sense of time, into a world beyond it. 

On more than any other release, his entire body of work to date can be experienced in a single statement. There are the seemingly random tonal structures that are such a large part of his vocabulary, the playfulness and humour of his formative noise schooling, his love of free jazz, of pop music, and rhythmic elements, perhaps subconsciously derived from his Sephardic heritage. Another outpouring of personal, intimate and enduring music from Oren Ambarchi.”

items.body:
Building out January's 'EUSEXUA' with an end-of-year sequel, FKA twigs deploys another selection of partially-cooked clubwise tasting plates with help from Pinkpantheress, Danny Harle, Batu, Mechatok and others.

'EUSEXUA' emerged following twigs' club experiences living in Prague and for all its attempts to depict the grubby Eastern Bloc techno experience, somehow failed to capture its amphetimine-laced anxiety. Almost universally acclaimed, the album vexed anyone who preferred the more mysterious, emotionally fluid writing she used to be so adept at a few years back. 2025 twigs is Madge decked out in all Adidas and to remind everyone she's still here before the EOY charts hit, 'EUSEXIA' has been blessed with its essential counterpart - 11 new tracks that are supposed to be the "soundtrack to the hours after the rave." 

Musically it presents a familiar narrative. Opener 'Love Crimes' tweaks Swiss producer balzacc30's grinding 4/4 until it buckles, and twigs uses the opportunity to lay it on thick. 'EUSEXUA Afterglow' wakes up when the sun cracks and its tempo starts to swing; twigs sounds more at home on Mechatok's So So Def-alike 'HARD' and Pinkpantheress turns up to sprinkle fairy dust on the decent 'Wild And Alone'. 'Touch A Girl' serves up a near beatless slice of euphoria and 'Predictable Girl' is almost hyperpop, its deep-fried 2-step knock distorted within an inch of its life.

Immaculately manicured.

items.body:
100% killer reissue of Bim Sherman’s self-released 1988 dub masterpiece ‘Ghetto Dub’, mixed by King Tubby, Prince Jammy and Adrian Sherwood who diffuse rhythms by The Roots Radics and Sly & Robbie, newly remastered for its first new edition in 30 years.

With 2nd hand prices understandably climbing into triple figures, this overdue first vinyl reissue will be mana to the fiends. It takes pride of place in an ongoing programme of resurrected Sherman aces to portray him at his most elusive and atmospheric, or as the hype sticker calls it, “a journey in echo and space”.

His legendarily tone is threaded thru the desk by a team of JA/UK titans with the man himself in the producer role, sifting cuts from his Century Records: a label set up in the Uk in 1984, after his move from Kingston, JA, to London, where he became a crucial figure in the On-U Sound crew after joining their 1979 tour, and would lend to classic Dub Syndicate cuts among others. 

The record’s renown has grown over the years since Sherman’s passing in 2000 and the effective dissolution of his label. Week-End Records now do a sterling job of preserving his legacy with this edition, richly representing the warmth and pressure of the OG in its entirety, from the clean-spurred, buoyant step of its title tune to moon-booted ‘Untitled Dub’, via the soul-tugging ace ’Station Dub’ with its unanswered doorbells, and best showcase of his voice in ‘Moving Dub’, another alright stepper in ‘World Dub’, the bloozy wooze of ‘Danger Dub’ and wickedly skewed Afro-lilt of ‘Tribulation Dub.’

All killer.

items.body:
With Aguayo’s Closer Musik classics still fond in the memory - despite more than 25 years having passed! - the chimeric Chilean boss of Cómeme gathers a new squad of international players for ‘Anenoa’, a helplessly diverse testament to his binds with pop, dance, Latin club music, and electronica, and strengths in collaboration, with Etienne Jaumet, Angel Deradoorian, Rafael Cohen (!!!), and Matt Karmil on board...

 

"Matias Aguayo returns with Anenoa, a vibrant and imaginative new album. Known for continually redefining the possibilities of electronic music,  Aguayo’s latest work expands his exploration of voice, rhythm, and collective experience — creating songs that invite participation as much as they reward listening.

Across more than two decades, Aguayo has remained one of the most inventive figures in contemporary electronic music. From co-founding the influential duo Closer Musik, to his long-standing creative relationship with Kompakt, and the creation of the genre-defying C meme label, Aguayo has consistently pushed dance music beyond  convention — blending raw electronics, storytelling, humor, and performance into something deeply human and alive.

Now based in Mexico, Aguayo’s music has absorbed the vibrant energy of community-driven dance culture. Much of Anenoa is sung in Spanish and shaped by a spirit o collaboration that runs throughout the record. Long known for building creative communities through his label and performances, Aguayo brings together a diverse group o artists across Latin America, Europe, and beyond, turning the album into a constellation of voices and perspectives."

items.body:
Bay Area rapper Sha Ray teams up with DJ Haram on her debut album, spitting bold, unapologetic sex raps over Haram's heady but hard-hitting industrial-tinged beats. Heavy duty material FFO Gangsta Boo, Debby Friday or BbyMutha.

Back in 2022, Haram caught Sha Ray on stage in Brooklyn and was immediately struck by her presence. When Sha Ray tapped her for beats later on, she was already sold, meeting again face-to-face at an Armand Hammer/DJ Haram show in Los Angeles not long afterwards. But the collaboration didn't happen in a single studio; 'Critical Thot' is the result of a lengthy period of back-and-forth between Haram in Brooklyn and Sha Ray, who would reply to Haram's beats with demo versions of tracks and notes. As these demos evolved into proper tracks, Haram and Sha Ray's relationship blossomed and 'Critical Thot' emerged - a record that's inspired by both artists' experiences of their role as women in the music industry. 

Haram's grown significantly as a producer in the last few years. Her solo debut 'Beside Myself' was clearly a milestone, but she's also been spotted providing beats for a slew of Backwoodz regulars, from billy woods and Elucid to Ghais Guevara and Fielded. And 'Critical Thot' offers her the scratchpad she needed to try out some of her most adventurous ideas. Sha Ray doesn't stutter on 'The Material' when Haram cuts strings to ribbons over stuttering voices, oscillating from fast to slow, and although she meets Haram's snakelike Memphis groove with similar energy on 'Champagne and Bouquets', she's impressively unfazed when Haram pivots at the midway point, adding fairyale strings and musicbox chimes. 

Oakland rapper Nappy Nina shows up on 'Hey Queen' alongside Brookyln's JWords and both join Sha Ray for an alien-voiced deadpan over one of Haram's most uncompromising beats, a squashed, industrial-tinged speedrun through techno's muckiest edges that'd give Brodinski a run for his money. On 'Strictly', meanwhile, Haram pushes up the tempo to a brisk Jersey bounce and Sha Ray's charisma spills from every rubbery kick. "This is for my bitches, strictly for the bitches," she hisses. There's no doubt.

items.body:
Nurse With Wound's sleaziest groovers are treated to 30+ year VIP reworks by Andrew Liles, Matthew Waldron (err.app. (ext)), Diarmuid MacDiarmada, and Jean-Jacques Birgé.

A fan fave since its ’94 release, the OG ‘Rock ’N’ Roll Station’ framed Steven Stapleton, Colin Potter and co. indulging, to-the-hilt, a sherm-huffing type of low down swagger surely indebted to Captain Beefheart as much as Jacques Berrocal. Its status as a proper NWW classic has been cemented over the decades, and now returns glazed with mucky moxie by key co-conspirators.

Sometime band member Matthew Waldron emphasises the grinding title tune’s blues roots with modal psych guitar and layers of squirming vox on the Gros Module version, while Dublin linchpin Diarmaid MacDiarmada condenses the fumes of ‘Finsbury Park, May 8th, 1 35pm (Worlds to Conquer)’ in an illicit workshop of cranky clangs and atmospheric enigma.

Key NWW figure Andrew Liles hews closer to the original industrial swag of the title tune, extending and smearing its brothel creep in deeply trippy ‘Strange Wax’ alternative, and French composer-film director Jean-Jacques Birgé rudely distends and kneads ‘A Silhouette & A Thumback (Dance in Hyperspace)’ to a disfigured crumple laced with lysergic potency.

Ace!

items.body:
Brannten Schnüre, the experimental dark folk group out of Würzburg, Germany's 2015 album, 'Sommer Im Pfirsichhain' back in print.

"Christian Schoppik composed and played all the music, Katie Rich whispers, recites and sings. Together they make astoundingly beautiful folk with a rich instrumentation leaning towards the atonal spectrum. Instrumental wanderings stand alongside Nico-esque poetry tales. Christian plays the accordeon and in some songs guitar and flute. Inspired by hierophants like Nový Svět and David Jackman, solemn song fragments (a lot of old greek rembetiko-recordings) are modified and looped, with additional instruments and voices being integrated later on. His music has been described as “surreal folkcollage” and “german hauntology”.

With the emergence of Schoppik’s second project, a dada cabaret called Agnes Beil in 2010, Brannten Schnüre moved closer to the song structures of its frivolous sibling. The songs of Schoppik’s latest creation Sommer im Pfirsichhain are further accompanied by a female singing voice, lending the pieces the voluptuous quality of a stickily tense midsummer. Sommer Im Pfirschhain (Summer In The Peachgrove) is the second part of a quartet of releases. The first being Aprilnacht which got released on Sic Sic Tapes last year. Part three Geträumt hab' ich vom Martinszug and part four will follow later.

Reference points are bands like Winter Family and Twinsistermoon. Music etched on folkloric, ritual elements transferred into the 21th century. Also worth mentioning is the hand-drawn artwork which is made by artist Gwénola Carrère."

items.body:
Described as a "tiny big band", Parasite Jazz are a French non-jazz trio who make heady genre-averse library music from tape loops, found objects and a few carefully picked instruments.

Parasite Jazz materialized in 2023 with their self-titled debut, an introductory set that veered sharply from medieval folk to cartoon trance and space rock. But they've developed significantly since then; after touring France for a few months, they've matured and grown into their roles, shifting away from carnivalesque abstraction towards dark, lounge-y exotica. It's the kind of gear that's hard to place: are we hearing samples, or is it a live band? Tamara Goukassova leads on violin, synth, ocarina, voice and objects, while Alexandre Larcier handles the samples and tape loops and Théo Delaunay makes up the rhythm section. And although 'Apocalypse (Egged Up)' sounds like a hold tone rendition of the 'Twin Peaks' love theme, the lengthy 'Mascara' is more like an electro samba improv jam, while 'Black Moon' sounds like Tortoise jamming with Jean-Claude Vannier. Not bad at all.

items.body:
Following January's IDM-influenced 'Giane 2' tape, Surf Gang founder Evilgiane returns with a bumper sequel to 2024's acclaimed #HEAVENSGATE that lashes together lightheaded collaborations with Nourished by Time, xaviersobased, Anysia Kim, Rico Nasty, Cash Cobain, Harto Falión and plenty more.

After working with MIKE and Earl Sweatshirt on the divisive (and in our opinion, very good) 'Pompeii // Utility' full-length, Surf Gang's currency has never been more valuable. So there's more riding on '#HEAVENSGATE VOL.2' than there was when the first tape hit and helped break a swathe of underground operatives who are now household names. This second volume is just as feature packed and just as uncompromisingly weird; Giane has already shown how eager he is to wobble rap's foundations and over 44 minutes and 23 tracks there's really nothing for East Coast purists. On opening track 'frog splash' there's at least a pulverized rap beat to work with, its kick clipped and high-end hacked at like it's been chomped on by a clew of digital worms. But this is exactly the web-native sound that Giane's almost singlehandedly engineered and it's the ideal playground for rapper Rockitneedspace, who veers off the grid as if he's being pulled by an invisible magnetic force.

Even better is 'Go Slow', a track with vocalist Bootee that plays like an update to Leila's timeless 'Like Weather' blueprint and the heartstring-pulling '<3', where Anysia Kym turns in a fragile performance over Giane's brittle N64 organs. Nourished by Time shows up on 'Karma Sutra', overlaying Giane's glitchy rhythm with gritty Joy Division guitars and grungy vocals and Giane pulls big-room EDM into the mix on 'strobe lights', diminishing its impact by ducking the neon synths and gated snares underneath xaviersobased's garbled rhymes. There's almost too much to absorb in a single sitting, but '#HEAVENSGATE VOL.2' isn't an artist album, it's a mixtape in the classic sense, providing a window into one of the US's most fertile scenes - one that's still very much in motion.

items.body:
Antwerp’s ace Cortizona label task Jlin, The Hafler Trio, Ossia, Legowelt, Peaking Lights and many more to rework the dry machine action of Belgian mainstay Walter Verdin.

Not even the best track on his ‘PingPong’ 2LP - that would be either ‘Aceton’ or ‘Sequence X’ - ‘Minimalise’ is nevertheless characteristic of Walter Verdin’s near-half century of synth pursuits that once saw him as part of Belgium’s 1983 Eur*vision entry, with Pas De Deux. Thus the track’s arid paucity of ingredients, of vox, bleep track and white noise, supplies mutable material for the remixers, who generally hew faithful to his asceticism and drily Belgian wits on another screwball set from the guess-again label, Cortizona.

The most impressive is Jlin’s propulsive future footwork take, fizzing with concentrated details and prone to wickedly wrong-foot the ‘floor in its ride intricacies, whilst The Hafler Trio play true to form and the track title with a curiously compressed and smeared slant on the same elements that uncannily gets under skin. Closer to home, Sagat emphasises a certain Lowlands gloom with a tense type of deconstructed D&B restraint, resolving in mutant offbeats, and Legowelt does his ‘80s sci-fi thing with vocoders and 808 halfstep.

Elsewhere Peaking Lights’ the Verdin to the ‘floor with a coldwave house reduction, Beton Brut puckers it up like one of Mumdnce & Logoos’ weightless ping jobs, DJ Marcelle does her freeform noise punk thing, replete with typical snip of The Fall, and Annelies Monseré lathers its lyrics into a mantric sound poem.

items.body:
In a blend of concrète collage and spoken word, Osàre! Editions boss Elena Colombi hails Hastings’ heritage of refusenik queer counter-culture with a richly informative, playfully witty, and fascinating mixtape appropriate to the collective’s analog newsletter medium and underground dissemination...

“Sarah's, Satins and Blades (The Way We Found Each Other) is a limited-edition cassette currently presented as part of Lemons, Laws & Secret Doors: A Hastings Queer History Collective Exhibition at Hastings Museum. Drawing on newsletters produced by the Campaign for Homosexual Equality Hastings Group (CHASTE) and the 1066 Gay Community Organisation between 1974 and 1989, the work is presented on a medium contemporary to these publications, echoing the routes they once travelled: from room to room, hand to hand.

The A-side brings together readings from the original newsletters, reflections from members of the Hastings Queer History Collective, and fragments of fast-changing music. Announcements, advice columns and calls to action sit alongside personal testimony, tracing how queer people lived, met, organised and communicated across generations.

Expanding beyond the exhibition, the cassette lingers in voice as a space of memory, exchange and connection. As both object and document, it proposes an archive that can move again: rewound, replayed and passed on through new networks of listening. Following the exhibition, the cassette will also enter Hastings Museum's permanent collection.

The B-side features a composition developed during a residency at Piedicavallo Festival, Italy. Written during a difficult period, it reflects on care, friendship, recovery and connection, offering a fitting coda to a work centred on queer resilience and collective memory.”

"Considered the most accomplished modern jazz harpist, Dorothy Ashby (1932-1986) established the harp as an improvising jazz instrument, beyond earlier use as a novelty or background orchestral instrument. Legendary ska missile by the originators - a proper knees up for all the family and ravers of all stripes

items.body:
Mika Vainio & Ilpo Väisänen’s prodigious 1st mission as Panasonic, originally issued in 1994, before the A went AWOL.

A real slice of history right here, presenting longer and harder versions of a cut that appeared in a shorter form on Mika’s Ø album ‘Metri’, co-credited to him and Ilpo, and here going longer and doubled up with another duo battering ram, ‘Murtaja’. Both tunes sound very much of their time, when European techno was forged tougher to demand, paralleling movements of harder Chicago house and Detroit warehouse techno.

In Panasonic’s case, the results were typically ascetic, mostly bleached of discernible melody beyond rhythmelodic cadence, and locked, bloody-minded, to icy tattoos that reflected their originals in Finnish warehouse parties, and would pin them on the international techno and electronic music maps. Trust that ‘Muuntaja’ still leaves welts from its distorted kicks, and contains subs primed to quake foundations, whilst the B-side is ideal for gnashing rave punks and bass drum fetishists.

items.body:
Deep south rap archaeology for smokers and gangstas: some of the earliest known Three 6 Mafia jams cut to wax, resplendent in cruddiest ferric lo-fi that still smacks

Originally cooked up on CD in ’99, at an early crest of Three 6 Mafia’s hugely influential run, ‘Underground Volume 1’ hustles a dozen deadly examples of the deep south rap sound coming into its own, adapting influence from local Memphis pioneer, DJ Spanish Fly’s low-slung 808 crack, to their own brand of what would be known as “horrorcore”, defined by the gulliest lyrics and supremely dank atmospheres, set to trunk-quake bass. As history has proven, their formula of trilling drum machines, slowed samples and mantric bars laid the groundwork for the dominant sound of hardcore, gangster and modern ATL rap. Consider this one essential for any rude rap fiends.

items.body:
On a lushly poised suite of synth-gilded fusions with santur string virtuosos, Ustad Nawab Khan & Naved Nawab Khan, Catalan shapeshifter Pedro Vian refers to the inventive Indian electronics of The NID tapes, via Ravi Shankar & Philip Glass duos, or new age trips of Ariel Kalma

"Recorded during an intense week of sessions at Pedro Vian’s studio in Barcelona, the album captures a rare and concentrated encounter between traditions, generations, and sonic languages.

Ustad Nawab Khan, a 9th-generation master of the santoor and founder of Raaga Science, has devoted his life to exploring the emotional and psychological dimensions of Indian raaga music. His philosophy, “Raag se Ras utpan” — the creation of emotional states through specific raagas — forms a conceptual backbone for the project. Carrying the lineage forward, Naved Nawab Khan represents the 10th generation, bringing a contemporary global awareness while remaining deeply rooted in classical tradition.

The Bubble of Love unfolds through four meditations that create a dialogue between ancient tonal systems and modern electronic exploration. In three of the four pieces, the chromatic subtleties and traditional scales of the santoor intertwine with Pedro Vian’s unexpected synthesizers and electronic textures. These compositions form a bridge between Occidental and Oriental musical worlds, where resonance becomes a shared language.

In the fourth and final meditation, the collaboration shifts toward a more experimental dimension. While maintaining the same instrumental foundation — santoor and electronics — Pedro Vian explores alternative notes and scale structures, expanding the harmonic field. This movement reflects both understanding and incomprehension, alignment and tension between cultures. Rather than resolving differences, the music inhabits them, transforming contrast into a space of discovery.

Released on Modern Obscure Music, The Bubble of Love is not merely a fusion record. It is a concentrated meeting point — lineage and futurism, discipline and experimentation — crystallized in a week of deep listening and creative exchange within an intimate studio environment. At moments, the record subtly echoes earlier attempts to translate ancient traditions through emerging technologies. It recalls the spirit of experimentation found in projects where Moog synthesis sought to interpret the tonal worlds of classical instruments — from the dialogues between Ravi Shankar and Philip Glass, to the exploratory journeys of Ariel Kalma, whose music continues to resonate powerfully in the very walls where this album was recorded.

In this broader historical context, The Bubble of Love also resonates with the pioneering electronic explorations documented in The NID Tapes — the collection of early Indian electronic works recorded between 1969 and 1972 at the National Institute of Design in Ahmedabad. Founded with the support of composer David Tudor, who installed a Moog modular system in 1969, the NID studio became a radical space of post-independence experimentation, where composers such as Gita Sarabhai, I.S. Mathur, Atul Desai, S.C. Sharma and Jinraj Joshipura explored analogue synthesis, tape collage, voice and field recording — forging a meeting point between Western and Indian avant-garde traditions. Uncovered and restored through the long-term research of British artist Paul Purgas, and later presented alongside the publication Subcontinental Synthesis: Electronic Music at the National Institute of Design, India 1969–1972, The NID Tapes revealed a visionary chapter in South Asia’s sonic imagination — one where electronic instruments did not replace tradition, but refracted it into new forms.

While separated by decades and geography, The Bubble of Love inhabits a similar philosophical terrain: not the fusion of opposites, but the coexistence of lineages — where electronic sound becomes not an imposition, but a listening device. A way of approaching tradition with curiosity rather than control. In this sense, the album stands both as a continuation and a renewal — a contemporary meditation on the enduring dialogue between heritage and experimentation, between memory and future sound."

items.body:
Bundled with sonograms, soundtrack visualisations and film stills, Carsten Nicolai's latest Alva Noto deployment is a soundtrack to his short film about Japanese textiles that attempts to connect acoustic frequency patterns with traditional weaving techniques.

Believe it or not, but Nicolai's always been interested in weaving. He was born in Chemnitz, a city that was at the heart of the East German textile industry, and has amassed a collection of over 1,000 historical textile patterns. So he was the obvious choice to collaborate with Hoosoo, a gallery in Kyoto that's been producing textiles since the 17th century. The main piece featured here is the soundtrack from 'Wave Weave', a short video work that Nicolai directed to capture Hosoo's unique weaving process and magnify the loom's machinery, showing the "algorithms and temporality embedded in textiles." Funnily enough, the imagery isn't too far removed from patterns Nicolai has been toying with for decades: dense, complex matrices of lines and geometric shapes that he shadows with his suitably austere glitches and elegant tones. 

But this isn't a particularly gloomy offering; far from it, in fact. Nicolai is sentimental about the subject matter and meets the textiles with awe-inspiring swells and pads, adding faint, mechanical rhythms only when necessary. 'Sono Obi Landscape', meanwhile, was made by converting the musical portion into sonograms, then using those images to create textiles. We can hear the sound on this release (and spy the accompanying visual work) and it follows its predecessor nearly, decelerating the rhythms and bringing out some of the more atmospheric tonal qualities. Honestly, it's the closest Nicolai has ever sounded to Boards of Canada.

items.body:
Verve Vault re-issue Coltrane's 1966 LP 'Ascension'.

"Ascension, released in 1966 on Impulse! Records, stands as one of John Coltrane’s most radical and influential works. Subtitled “Edition I & II” to reflect the two complete takes recorded at the session—and presented together on LP for the first time—the piece is a nearly 40-minute large-ensemble performance marking Coltrane’s decisive embrace of the avant-garde. Recorded on June 28, 1965, at Rudy Van Gelder’s Englewood Cliffs studio and produced by Bob Thiele, the session assembled an expanded ensemble of eleven musicians. Alongside Coltrane’s tenor saxophone are trumpeters Freddie Hubbard and Dewey Johnson; saxophonists Pharoah Sanders, Marion Brown, John Tchicai, and Archie Shepp; pianist McCoy Tyner; bassists Art Davis and Jimmy Garrison; and drummer Elvin Jones. The music alternates between densely textured collective improvisation and extended solo statements, conjuring a hurricane of violent, searching sound. Initially controversial for its intensity and freedom, Ascension has since come to be recognized as a landmark of modern jazz and a defining statement of the emerging free-jazz movement. Presenting both takes together highlights the organic, ever-changing character of the performance and affirms its enduring place in Coltrane’s artistic legacy."

items.body:
A pair of Europe’s finest DJs go toe-to-toe for 80 mins at Portugal’s renowned Lux Fragil Festival, ribboning myriad strands of trippy techno-house to acidic electro and body music with hypnotic traction.

Not their first rodeo - they’ve gone b2b at Dekmantel and on radio - ‘Live At Lux Fragil, 2026’ finds the pair of respective club sorceresses in fluid simpatico, matching each other for killer obscurities and slept-on gems from the back shelves of club music. 

The first 40 mins slinks from proto-Goa types of new beat and breaks-driven Euro house to bittersweet electro prongs and darker strains of UK electro as they find their range, before the 2nd side shifts up a gear into haughtier body music and deep, tracky bangers, riddled with pinging screwballs.

In other words: a real knees-up.

items.body:
Ricardo Villalobos runs rings around two trax from goat (JP)’s 2025 dance score in three durational, tempo-sloped parts for Paris-based Latency. Japanese no wave asceticism meets haughty house trot and lizard-hipped slink - 35 mins of it!

In their own ways, both Ricky V and Goat (JP) are no strangers to the weirder ends of the ‘floor, each excelling at threading the most sinuous grooves to the most fanciful purposes. Now brought together by Parisian electronic atelier Latency, Villalobos pursues his preceding reworks of Reza Mortazevi’s hand-played percussion with a supple loosening of goat (jp)’s crystalline pulses in three distinct variations, tweaking the original timbales of ‘Orin’ away from avant-dance roots into 9 mins of heavily infectious wiggle swarmed with class, over-the-shoulder vocals, kinda something from his ‘Sei Es Drum’ series. ‘Factory’ on the other hand is taken for a longer ride in contrasting parts, recalibrating its cogs with a grittier swivel and unravelled loops of the OG in Variation 1, then slowing it all to a superb 110BPM version bound for the *special* folder and loosey goosey ends of the day/night.

items.body:
Seattle-based electronica artist Hünter makes a strong first impression with their debut volley of intricately amorphous rhythms and probing tones, in arrangements blending club, neo-classical, and sound designer urges, FFO Svbkvlt, Æ, Björk

“Of Paradise welcomes Seattle-based artist Hünter with his sophomore album, Mica, a sublime addition to the label’s ever-evolving musical catalogue and one that quickly acquires almost mythical status.

Focused on the relationship between the digital age and the environment, Mica explores the extraction of natural resources, identity, memory, and what remains. A fusion of ambient soundscapes and deconstructed club rhythms, Mica questions erosion as both a physical and cultural consequence of modern consumption, encouraging listeners to reevaluate their relationship with nature, technology, and excess.

Available as a limited edition 12” and digital album, Mica responds to overstimulation; music that breathes slowly, punctuated by occasional moments of tension, provides periods of stillness and reflection interrupted by the intensity of digital life and environmental anxiety. This album isn’t merely a collection of songs; it’s an atmosphere to inhabit.”

UR’s live percussionist displays his range on this 2011 EP; from hi-tech jazz swag to haughty stomp and a broken beat killer, all packing proper Motor City techno soul

Mark Flash’s reputation precedes him as a staple UR member for decades, as well as a crackshot DJ and producer, as heard here. His ‘King of Light’ is cut from finest Mad Mike-type tekkerz, brimming with optimistic melody and heart-lifting string harmonies on a driving house groove. ‘Dark Symphony’ plays to his tuffer side with something closer to Suburban Knight archetypes, but also compatible with strains of upfront UKF, and, best of all, ‘Eagle Warriors’ really flexes his drummer chops in its tight, rolling breaks, electro punctuation, and stately string/synth arrangement.

Timeless lovers pearl by the sister of Alton Ellis, as heard in Steve McQueen’s gorgeous depiction of the early ‘80s lovers era on the Small Axe series

The original endures as an all time Lovers classic, Hortense drizzling honey on super laid-back but buoyant sway. The version is sparser, bringing up the nagging rhythm guitar and horn melody to get lost in.

items.body:
Patrick Gräser, AKA Answer Code Request, was one of the defining producers of Berghain's second generation.  First emerging  in the early '10s, Gräser was producing industrial-strength techno influenced by the hardcore continuum, serving Berlin techno with a twist of UK rave and '90s IDM. 

As a resident of the Berlin club, he was an heir apparent to mentor Marcel Dettmann—only instead of Dettmann's penchant for EBM and new wave, it sounded like Gräser had spent formative years clubbing on Fridays during the Sub:stance heydays. The pair of records he released during that period—2014's    Code   and 2018's   Gens  —remain high watermarks of the Ostgut Ton catalogue. 

New LP  Halo  picks up where  Gens  left off. The synth work alternates between chillout tent comedown and Japanese-school psychedelia, where the melodies seem to twist and turn in on themselves. The sweeping chords on "Shine Deep" are borderline too celestial, but just when we're about to drift off into the ether, Gräser spices up the break with a kick drum that sounds lifted out of a Shed record. 

The title track, on the other hand, hews closer to something DJ Nobu might play. "Halo" starts with what sounds like an army of buzzing cybernetic mosquitos trapped in a closet seeking out blood, before unleashing a closed hi-hat and freewheeling bassline halfway through. It transforms the track into a proper barnstormer, as well as being a callback to an era-specific Berlin techno sound. 

Gräser remains able to infuse a wide range of emotional depth into the austere templates of techno. There's plenty of that across  Halo  (see also the Autechre synth squiggles and syncopated groove on "Bliphar"). But he also pushes himself out of his comfort zone: "D-Fracture" is like listening to a techno remake of Ed Rush and Optical's dark drum & bass classic,  Wormhole , as the creeping feedback consumes the stereo field like a horror movie garbage disposal. 

The opener, "Fading Shadows", also lets Gräser write the  Selected Ambient Works  song he's always wanted (in fact, the track might be even better without the kick drum that eventually does come in). These aren't necessarily new tricks, but a sign that Gräser isn't resting on his laurels just yet. 

Times have changed since Gräser first released music, when Berghain and Ostgut Ton represented a sonic vanguard. The club is no longer the musical weathervane it once was, even as it remains a cultural flashpoint.  But it's also true that the Berghain sound was never monolithic. 

Nostalgia might have us all imagine it was cold, steely minimalism from Saturday to Monday afternoon, but things were always weirder. Hell, just listen to Dettmann's jump cut to Kevin Saunderson's "Just Want Another Chance" on   Berghain 002  , or go to a recent REEF party for that matter.  Gräser, in this sense, embodies the club's more wide-ranging ethos. While  Halo  may not represent the future of techno, it still showcases one of the best producers of the past 20 years.
